stimulus.text: After 1676, Virginia's planters stopped trusting a workforce that could unite across race. White servants were politically fractious, and fewer English workers were willing to endure southern farm labor when better work could be found in the northern colonies. At the same time, the Dutch monopoly on the slave trade ended in 1682, and the price of enslaved Africans fell. A workforce held for life, whose children were born into bondage, gave planters something servants never could: workers who could never claim the liberties of Englishmen and never walk away free.
stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, summarizing 5 Steps 2024 Ch 8 and Princeton Review Ch 6.

books.section: Bacon's Rebellion and the Development of Slavery in Virginia

stem: In the late 1600s, Chesapeake planters increasingly purchased enslaved Africans rather than contracting indentured servants. Which of the following best explains this shift?

options.text: Lifetime enslavement gave planters a permanent workforce for tobacco fields.
The English crown offered tax rebates to planters who bought enslaved Africans.
Indentured servants collectively refused to work in tobacco fields after Bacon's Rebellion.
options.misconception: Servants did not boycott tobacco work; their supply shrank for economic reasons in England.

options.text: A surplus of enslaved laborers in New England drove prices down in southern markets.
options.misconception: New England had very few enslaved people and no surplus to send south.

rationales.general:
1. Name what a planter needed. Workers for tobacco, season after season, who would not walk away free.
2. Compare the two workforces. A servant's term ended; an enslaved person's bondage lasted for life, and their children were born into it.
3. Ask what changed the price. The Dutch monopoly on the slave trade ended in 1682, and enslaved Africans got cheaper just as servants got scarcer.
4. Put the two together. Lifetime labor, cheaper to buy, solved the planter's problem twice over.
Remember: a labor system changes when both the politics and the price point the same way.
rationales.A: Enslaved Africans could be held for life, and their children were born into slavery, giving planters a permanent, self-reproducing workforce for the tobacco fields. Servants' terms ended. Background: servants who survived wanted land of their own, a problem after Bacon's Rebellion showed the poor could unite. Lifetime enslavement solved both problems: workers who never walked away free. The other options are wrong: no crown rebates existed, servants did not boycott tobacco work, and New England had no enslaved surplus to send south.
rationales.B: No royal tax rebates for purchasing enslaved laborers existed.
rationales.C: Servants did not boycott tobacco work; the servant supply shrank for economic reasons in England.
rationales.D: New England had a small enslaved population and no surplus to send south.
